name: IPL photofacial

lead: An IPL photofacial fades sun spots, freckles, uneven pigmentation, redness and visible small blood vessels, leaving a clearer, more even complexion.

A handheld flashlamp emits brief pulses of broad-spectrum light, roughly 400 to 1200 nm, which melanin, haemoglobin and water absorb and convert to heat. This damages the targeted pigment or vessel, which the body then clears, while cooling protects the surface. Reviews describe it as working well for pigmentation and vascular lesions and less well for wrinkles. The FDA cleared it for vascular lesions in 1995, pigmented lesions in 1996 and hair removal in 1997.

paras: It is a mainstream dermatology and aesthetic treatment done in clinics, usually as a short series of sessions, with filters chosen for the concern. Home devices are also sold.

Reported complications include hyperpigmentation, temporary redness, burns and microscopic thermal injury. Photosensitising medications and existing skin damage are listed as contraindications. A manufacturer cited in one source recommends use mainly on light to medium skin tones, since darker skin carries higher risk.

chain: Light pulses target pigment and vessels
angle.text: IPL photofacials are used to fade sun spots, uneven pigmentation, redness and visible small blood vessels for a clearer, more even complexion. Light pulses are absorbed by pigment and blood vessels, which break down and fade. Reviews describe it as working well for pigmentation and vascular concerns and less well for wrinkles.

lead: An IPL photofacial, also called photorejuvenation, is a cosmetic and dermatological treatment that uses intense pulsed light (IPL) to improve skin affected by sun damage, uneven pigmentation, redness and visible small blood vessels. A computer-controlled handheld flashlamp emits brief pulses of non-coherent, broad-spectrum light, roughly 400 to 1200 nm, which targets melanin, haemoglobin and water in the skin.[1]

Unlike lasers, which emit a single wavelength, IPL devices use interchangeable filters so that one machine can be used for several conditions. The technology was invented by Shimon Eckhouse in 1992, and the US FDA cleared it for vascular lesions in 1995, pigmented lesions in 1996 and hair removal in 1997.[1]
Reviews of photorejuvenation methods describe IPL as working well for pigmentation and blood-vessel lesions but less well for wrinkles, with limited or anecdotal safety data in places.[2]
infobox: Vascular lesions 1995; pigmented lesions 1996; hair removal 1997[1]
Sun spots, freckles, redness, broken capillaries, rosacea

paras: Encyclopedia summaries list photorejuvenation and sun damage (dyspigmentation, sun-related vascular changes, melasma and skin laxity), rosacea and acne-related concerns, telangiectasia and pigmented lesions such as freckles and liver spots.[1][2] IPL is also used for hair removal and for dry eye caused by meibomian gland dysfunction.[1] Wikipedia's page on skin rejuvenation lists dyschromia, rosacea, melasma, acne, photodamage, vascular and pigmented lesions and wrinkles among conditions treated.[2]

A 2004 multi-centre study described IPL as a non-invasive, non-ablative method with minimal adverse events, and IPL is reported to work well for pigmentation and blood-vessel lesions but less well for wrinkles.[2] For hair removal, a 2006 study found no statistically significant difference at six months between IPL, alexandrite and diode lasers, though IPL is generally described as less effective than laser hair removal; typical courses take about 8 to 10 sessions several weeks apart.[1]

The most notable complication is hyperpigmentation, and side effects in the 2006 comparison were generally temporary, occurring in 15.3 percent of IPL-treated participants against 28.9 percent for the diode laser.[1] Photosensitising medications and existing skin damage are contraindications, and the treated area should be free of sunburn.[1] Some studies have found that direct heat can damage DNA in treated and nearby cells, causing microscopic thermal injury, and the evidence base includes anecdotal reports.[2] A manufacturer cited by Wikipedia recommends use mainly on light to medium skin tones.[1]

Rules differ by jurisdiction. Some jurisdictions distinguish beauty-grade from medical-grade devices, a distinction Wikipedia notes is sometimes used to avoid regulation. Home IPL devices are sold to consumers.[1]

Human studies include a 2004 multi-centre study of IPL photorejuvenation reporting minimal adverse events[2] and a 2006 comparison of IPL with alexandrite and diode lasers for hair reduction.[1] Dedicated trials of photofacials specifically in looksmaxxing-motivated populations were not found.
The treatment was added to the wiki as a light therapy for sun damage within the hardmaxx category. No looksmaxxing community material is available to document how it is discussed there.

timeline.event: Shimon Eckhouse invents and patents intense pulsed light.[1]
